parts: Lesson 15: Management of Time and Energy — Summary

Time and energy are limited resources used together. Time is equal for everyone (24 hours); energy is the capacity to do work and differs from person to person. Making the best use of them is time and energy management; taking a short cut saves both.

A time plan or schedule is an advance plan of what we are going to do in a given period. Steps: (1) list all the activities; (2) group them into flexible activities (shopping – can be shifted) and inflexible activities (school, classes – fixed time); (3) estimate the time required for each activity; (4) balancing – adjusting the time of activities so that the total fits the available time (reduce time on some activities; start with activities that take long). Points to keep in mind: a schedule easy to follow, practical and flexible, an alternative plan for emergencies, time for rest and leisure, dovetailing. Peak load periods are times of the day when many activities have to be done in a fixed time (morning); manage them by pre-preparation (iron uniforms and prepare food in the evening). Leisure period is the rest and hobby time that recharges the body and relieves stress. Family members' plans that clash are adjusted (bathing order).

Advantages of a time plan: finish all work efficiently without tiredness; find time for rest and hobbies; do more productive and better quality work in less time; avoid last-minute tension and confusion; time for unforeseen events such as visitors or illness. Ways to save time: follow the plan, do not waste time, use labour-saving equipment, and dovetail.

Dovetailing is doing two or three activities at the same time. Example: cooking dal and vegetables, washing dishes and washing clothes one after another takes 20 + 20 + 20 + 20 = 80 minutes; by dovetailing (start the washing machine, put the dal on to boil, cut vegetables while washing runs, wash dishes while cooking) the same work takes 5 + 2 + 5 + 10 + 20 + 5 + 8 = 55 minutes, saving 25 minutes.

Heavy activities need much energy (running, jogging, mopping, Diwali cleaning, cycling); moderate need an average amount (sweeping, ironing, cooking, preparing notes); light need very little (reading, watching TV, listening to music, telling a story). Fatigue can be physical or mental. Ways to save energy (work simplification): break a task into smaller activities (washing clothes: separate, soak, rub, rinse, dry); cut extra movements and combine activities (serve all glasses on a tray; clear the table in one or two trips); do activities in a better order (sweep before hanging clothes; dust before sweeping the floor is wrong); be skilled; use the correct posture (long-handled broom instead of bending, sit erect while studying); work at proper heights and keep things near the place of use (put things back); use labour-saving devices (mixer, toaster).
